author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Abortion on OUR terms
content:
Everyone deserves access to abortion care when and where they need it — without judgment, stigma, or shame. Because of abortion stigma and the ongoing threat to abortion access, it is difficult to find reliable and clear information on abortion, a common medical process that one in four women in the U.S. will have before age 45. There is no “right” or “wrong” reason to choose to have an abortion, and it’s okay to have several. You are trusted with understanding your life and your needs.

“An unintended pregnancy is not a weakness or a moral failing but an inevitable occurrence in a society hell-bent on keeping you as vulnerable and unprotected as possible. You didn’t fuck up. You’re not irresponsible. You don’t need to bear any ‘consequences’ or be punished.” — Hannah Matthews (@hannahmsays)

These resources can help you get started determining what type of abortion might work best for you, where to find an appointment, and organizations that can support with appointment costs or practical support for travel if you need to leave your home state to receive care.

Medication Abortion: Mifepristone, a pill, is usually taken with an abortion provider while at the clinic, while Misoprostol, another type of pill, is taken 24-48 hours later inside your own home.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Practicing Consent
content:
We might broadly define consent as a wholehearted and mutual ongoing agreement between parties and/or individuals towards a common goal. Consent lies at the crux of radical imaginings. Practicing consent is all the more important since we did not consent to capitalism. In a world of non-consent, consent becomes radical.

But what is consent? We often hear about consent in terms of sexual praxis. Consent is saying “yes,” asking/waiting for the emphatic “yes,” and listening to “no.” It is practicing boundaries, both towards oneself and others. However, consent is more than that. Consent is an ongoing and nuanced exchange. Consent can be ephemeral and allows itself to be invoked, revoked and tailored to complex, evolving situations. Consent is a conversation and demands a back and forth. Consent challenges us to lay our desires bare at the feet of our lovers and comrades while centering their desires with our own.

Consent may best be defined as a harmonious understanding between all parties involved. Some things we can do to be better at consensual, harmonious engagement include:

• Being honest about our own desires and limits

• Sticking to our own boundaries

• Honestly acknowledging the boundaries of others

• Predicting changes in boundaries when possible

• Asking for continuous feedback

• Being open and enthusiastic about receiving feedback!

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Mental Health Reminders
content:
These are dark times. It is, in fact, the world that is crazy – despair and anxiety are natural responses to watching society destroy itself for the wealthy and powerful. But by reaching out to each other, we can find the courage to stay engaged with the world, to survive, and to fight back. Mental health and mental health crises vary a lot between people, and are often intertwined with class, race, gender, and activism. These suggestions are generic, but may be useful for yourself or others. If you find yourself or someone you love having delusional thinking or consider self-harm or other violence, these suggestions probably aren’t enough. Remember that it is okay to reach out for professional help!

• Our brains are connected to our bodies, so physical health can help with mental distress. Eating healthy food on a regular schedule and getting enough sleep are necessary for mental stability and sustained activism. Exercise, dance, and physical movement help, too. So can fresh air and having a stable, calming place to stay. Try to recognize if you’re missing one of these, and if that’s causing distress.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Live in the Real World
content:
Our dependence on our phones isn’t an accident. We depend on them logistically for our navigation, payment, and communication. But our phones and the apps they contain are also designed to build emotional dependence — there are entire teams of top-of-their-field psychologists, engineers, sociologists, and designers getting paid hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to make apps even just a little bit more addictive. The emotional and logistical dependence on our phones intertwine in a mutual feedback loop, making it difficult to reduce either.

Every interaction we have with our phones deepens opportunities for state surveillance. Our online activity creates a database of our interests, purchase history, friend networks, location, and activism that the FBI of yesteryear could only have dreamed of. But the biggest problem, as with any addiction, is how something that is fun and useful in small doses can start to take more and more of our time and attention, preventing us from doing other things that we value. So what is there to do?

For most of us, the apps that most deeply build psychological dependence on our phones are social media apps and games. These often take, in some ways, the place of cigarettes in our society today — we do them on a quick break, or when we need to ‘unwind’. author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Supporting a friend in jail
content:
The systems of oppression operated by the 1% are vulnerable — they are unsustainable and they can be defeated — but they won’t crumble on their own. People just like us help with protests, riots, middle of the night missions and other acts of resistance. Affinity groups are small direct action cells — usually 4-8 people — who share attitudes about tactics and who organize themselves during actions for effectiveness and protection. Affinity groups can organize actions or make them better once the actions are underway.

Many affinity groups choose a legal support person for each action who stays at another location to avoid possible arrest, so they can handle things if members of the group are arrested. Jail aims to isolate and disempower us so we’ll sit down and shut up. But when we support each other, we can resist and return to the streets stronger. Here are some brief tips for being a jail support person.

• Agree on a phone number that accepts collect calls to call if someone gets arrested and then be at that number.

• Make a list of the real full name, arrest history, outstanding warrants, emergency contacts, and other special needs of each member such as kids that need childcare, medical needs, doctor’s names, etc. Note if a person’s chosen name is different than the one on their ID and if there is a concern that they might be held in housing that does not match their gen

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Radical Response Networks
content:
Panic and paranoia are counterproductive — stop wondering what will happen, or why nothing’s happening. If we’re going to survive the ongoing collapse of capital and empire, we need to be able to identify our goals and catalyze the conditions they require.

Communities under threat from repressive institutions have been coming together for emergency self-defense and found out that they ended up with something even more important — a renewed sense of community care, trust in neighbors and inspiration.

Rapid response networks aim to document, obstruct, and expose to public scorn harmful federal, police and government repression. They can take the form of individual escorts, neighborhood watches, horizontally organized information sharing networks, or entire sub-communities ready to act effectively as they see fit.

Effective networks are composed of many different types of people from all walks of life: neighbors, coworkers, classmates. Anyone who frequently occupies, passes by, or visits endangered areas can provide eyes on the ground. Networks reach out to out high risk community members and figure out where support is most needed. Some communities conduct security trainings, legal support sessions, or mutual aid distribution for affected community members.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Know your rights with COPS
content:
These suggestions from the National Lawyers Guild “Know Your Rights” guide summarize the rules to which the police are theoretically subject. Be careful: the police, the courts, and the government can and do ignore these rules when they feel like it. Sometimes, police retaliate against people for exercising their rights. These tips may help you later on in court, and sometimes they won’t. Even though the state can’t be counted on to follow its own laws, it still may be helpful to know what these laws are so you can shame particular state agents or deal with particular situations. Use your best judgment — if you aren’t doing anything wrong, there may be no reason to be excessively paranoid or escalate a potentially innocent and brief encounter with a police officer who is just saying “hi” into an ugly situation by acting suspicious and refusing to say “hi” back. The point is to avoid giving information.

Providing this information isn’t intended to scare you into inactivity or make you paranoid. In the current context, the vast majority of radical projects proceed with no interference from the police. The police hassle and arrest people because they hope that such repression will frighten everyone else into submission. We can take reasonable precautions while continuing the fight for liberation.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Prison pen pals
content:
Support for people in prison can include books-to-prisoners projects that mail free books, or individually becoming pen-pals with a person in prison. Some people focus on political prisoners, while others see the entire prison-industrial complex as illegitimate and criticize the way that it targets marginalized communities. A key way we can support people inside is by communicating with them. In an email-dominated world, writing an old-fashioned letter on paper can be surprisingly rewarding for you as well as an incarcerated person. Here are some tips.

• When writing to people in prison, put their prisoner number on the first line of the mailing address to get it through.

• Make sure to put a return address on your letter. If you are writing to a prisoner you don’t know, it may be best to use a PO box or other address that doesn’t disclose where you live.

• If you’re writing to an incarcerated person, keep in mind that the prison officials or other authorities will read your letter. Don’t discuss anything sensitive. If the person is waiting for trial or sentencing (or on appeal), it may be better not to discuss the details of their case.

• Prisons prohibit mailing items like food, money, and sometimes books — ask your pen-pal for the rules.
